sections.name: 1.1 Flower - A Fascinating Organ of Angiosperms

concepts.text: Flowers as sites of sexual reproduction; aesthetic, ornamental, social and cultural value
Pre-fertilisation events begin with hormonal and structural changes leading to floral primordium
Androecium (whorl of stamens) and gynoecium (pistil) as male and female reproductive organs
1.2.1 Stamen: filament and bilobed anther, dithecous; four microsporangia at corners
Microsporangium wall layers: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum (nourishes pollen; dense cytoplasm, often multinucleate)
Sporogenous tissue; microsporogenesis - microspore mother cells divide by meiosis forming microspore tetrads
Pollen grain structure: exine of sporopollenin (most resistant organic material) with germ pores; intine of cellulose and pectin
Mature pollen: vegetative cell (large, food reserve) and generative cell (spindle-shaped); shed at 2-celled (60% of angiosperms) or 3-celled stage
Pollen viability (rice/wheat 30 min; Rosaceae, Leguminosae, Solanaceae months); pollen allergy (Parthenium/carrot grass); pollen tablets as food supplement
Pollen banks: cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen (-196 C)
1.2.2 The pistil, megasporangium (ovule) and embryo sac: monocarpellary vs multicarpellary, apocarpous (Michelia) vs syncarpous (Papaver)
Ovule structure: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac
Megasporogenesis: megaspore mother cell meiosis gives four megaspores; one functional
Female gametophyte development: monosporic; three mitotic divisions give 8-nucleate, 7-celled embryo sac
Embryo sac organisation: egg apparatus (two synergids with filiform apparatus + egg cell), three antipodals, central cell with two polar nuclei
1.2.3 Pollination: transfer of pollen to stigma; autogamy, geitonogamy, xenogamy
Chasmogamous vs cleistogamous flowers (Viola, Oxalis, Commelina); assured seed set in cleistogamy
Agents of pollination: abiotic (wind, water) and biotic (animals)
Wind pollination features: light non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens, large feathery stigma, single ovule, numerous flowers in inflorescence (corn cob tassels)
Water pollination: Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera; mucilaginous covering on pollen; water hyacinth and lily are insect/wind pollinated despite aquatic habitat
Insect/animal pollination: bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds, hummingbirds), bats; large colourful fragrant nectar-rich flowers; sticky pollen
Floral rewards (nectar, pollen) and specific associations: Yucca and moth, Amorphophallus; pollen/nectar robbers

Outbreeding devices: pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised, different positions of anther and stigma, self-incompatibility, unisexual flowers (castor, maize - monoecious; papaya - dioecious)
Pollen-pistil interaction: recognition of compatible pollen; pollen tube growth through style to micropyle; entry via synergid's filiform apparatus
Artificial hybridisation: emasculation (removal of anthers), bagging, rebagging; used in crop improvement
Exercise type: list the stages of microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis; ploidy of different cells/tissues
Syngamy: one male gamete fuses with egg to form diploid zygote
Triple fusion: second male gamete fuses with two polar nuclei forming triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)
Double fertilisation unique to flowering plants; central cell becomes primary endosperm cell
1.4.1 Endosperm: development precedes embryo; PEN divides to form triploid nutritive tissue; free-nuclear endosperm (coconut water) then cellular (white kernel)
Endosperm fully consumed (pea, groundnut, beans) or persists (castor, coconut, cereals)
1.4.2 Embryo: develops at micropylar end; proembryo, globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo stages
Dicot embryo: embryonal axis with two cotyledons, epicotyl (plumule), hypocotyl (radicle)
Monocot embryo: one cotyledon (scutellum), coleoptile, coleorhiza
1.4.3 Seed: fertilised ovule with seed coat, cotyledons, embryo axis; non-albuminous vs albuminous seeds; perisperm (black pepper, beet)
Seed dormancy and maturation; seed coats from integuments; micropyle allows O2 and water entry
Fruit development: ovary wall becomes pericarp; true fruits vs false fruits (apple, strawberry, cashew - thalamus contributes)
Parthenocarpic fruits (banana) formed without fertilisation; induced by growth hormones
Advantages of seeds: independent of water for pollination, dispersal adaptations, food reserves, dormancy, genetic variation; seed viability (lupine 10,000 years, date palm 2000 years)
Apomixis: seed formation without fertilisation (asexual reproduction mimicking sexual); in some Asteraceae and grasses
Ways of apomixis: diploid egg cell formed without reduction division; nucellar cells developing into embryos (citrus, mango)
Polyembryony: more than one embryo in a seed (orange)
Importance of apomixis for hybrid seed industry - hybrid traits preserved without segregation
Exercise type: explain double fertilisation and endosperm development; differentiate geitonogamy and xenogamy; give examples of outbreeding devices
Exercise type: label diagrams of anther T.S., pollen, anatropous ovule, embryo sac, monocot and dicot embryo
Humans are sexually reproducing and viviparous; events: gametogenesis, insemination, fertilisation, cleavage and implantation, gestation, parturition
Reproductive events after puberty; age-related changes in gamete production between sexes
Testes in scrotum (temperature 2-2.5 C lower than body); testicular lobules with seminiferous tubules
Seminiferous tubule lining: male germ cells (spermatogonia) and Sertoli cells (nourish germ cells); interstitial Leydig cells secrete androgens
Accessory ducts: rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra; penis with glans and foreskin
Accessory glands: paired seminal vesicles, prostate, paired bulbourethral glands; seminal plasma rich in fructose, calcium, enzymes
Diagram skill: labelled diagram of male reproductive system and T.S. of seminiferous tubule
Ovaries (primary sex organs) produce ovum and hormones; ovarian stroma with cortex and medulla
Accessory ducts: oviducts (fallopian tubes - infundibulum with fimbriae, ampulla, isthmus), uterus, vagina
Uterus wall: perimetrium, myometrium (smooth muscle, strong contractions at delivery), endometrium (cyclic changes)
External genitalia: mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen, clitoris; hymen's presence not an indicator of virginity
Mammary glands: glandular tissue in lobes with alveoli, mammary tubules, ducts, ampulla, lactiferous duct
Spermatogenesis: spermatogonia (2n) -> primary spermatocytes -> secondary spermatocytes (n, meiosis I) -> spermatids (meiosis II)
Spermiogenesis: transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa; spermiation (release from seminiferous tubules)
Hormonal control: GnRH from hypothalamus; LH acts on Leydig cells (androgens), FSH acts on Sertoli cells (spermiogenesis factors)
Sperm structure: head (haploid nucleus, acrosome), neck, middle piece (mitochondria), tail; 200-300 million sperms per ejaculation, 60% normal shape, 40% vigorous motility
Oogenesis: begins in foetal stage - oogonia form primary oocytes arrested in prophase I; primary follicles; many degenerate before puberty
Follicular development: primary, secondary, tertiary (antrum, theca externa/interna), Graafian follicle
Secondary oocyte formed with first polar body (unequal division); zona pellucida; ovulation releases secondary oocyte
Comparison table: spermatogenesis vs oogenesis (number of gametes, timing, polar bodies)
Menstrual cycle in primates; menarche (first menstruation) and menopause (~50 years); average 28/29 days
Menstrual phase (3-5 days): breakdown of endometrium; absence indicates pregnancy or other causes
Follicular (proliferative) phase: follicle growth, endometrium regeneration; FSH and LH rise; oestrogen secretion
Ovulatory phase: LH surge around day 14 induces Graafian follicle rupture
Luteal (secretory) phase: corpus luteum secretes progesterone maintaining endometrium; degenerates without fertilisation
Graph interpretation: levels of pituitary and ovarian hormones and ovarian/uterine events through the cycle
Insemination during coitus; sperm and ovum meet at ampullary region of fallopian tube
Fertilisation: sperm contacts zona pellucida, blocks polyspermy; secondary oocyte completes meiosis II forming ovum and second polar body; zygote formed
Sex of baby decided by sperm carrying X or Y chromosome (XX female, XY male)
Cleavage: mitotic divisions producing blastomeres, morula (8-16 cells), blastocyst
Blastocyst: outer trophoblast and inner cell mass (gives rise to embryo); implantation into endometrium
Chorionic villi and uterine tissue form placenta; umbilical cord connection
Placental functions: nutrient/O2 supply, removal of CO2 and wastes, endocrine role
Pregnancy hormones: hCG, hPL, oestrogens, progestogens from placenta; relaxin from ovary; increased levels of other maternal hormones
Germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm from inner cell mass; stem cells with potency to give all tissues/organs

Developmental milestones: heart at 1 month; limbs and digits by 2nd month; major organs by 12 weeks (first trimester); movements and hair by 5th month; eyelids and eyelashes by 24 weeks; 9-month gestation
Parturition: vigorous contraction of uterus at end of pregnancy; foetal ejection reflex triggered by foetus and placenta
Oxytocin release from maternal pituitary causes stronger contractions; positive feedback
Lactation: mammary glands produce milk; colostrum rich in antibodies (IgA) gives early immunity
Exercise type: draw labelled diagrams of male/female reproductive systems, sperm, Graafian follicle, blastocyst; explain hormonal regulation of menstrual cycle
Exercise type: compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis; trace events from fertilisation to implantation; true/false statements on reproductive anatomy
WHO definition: total well-being in physical, emotional, behavioural and social aspects of reproduction
India among first countries with national family planning programme (1951); RCH (Reproductive and Child Health Care) programmes
Strategies: awareness through audio-visual and print media, sex education in schools, information on STDs, care of pregnant mothers, gender equality
Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination to check female foeticide; amniocentesis for genetic disorder detection
Research on contraceptives; improved reproductive health indicators (lower maternal and infant mortality, small families, better care for STDs)
Population explosion causes: decline in death rates, MMR and IMR; increase in reproductive-age population
Census data: about 350 million in 1947 to over a billion by 2000; growth rate decreasing
Measures: raising marriageable age (18 for females, 21 for males), incentives for small families
Ideal contraceptive: user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible, few side effects, no interference with libido
Natural methods: periodic abstinence (days 10-17), coitus interruptus/withdrawal, lactational amenorrhoea
Barrier methods: condoms (male and female, also protect from STIs), diaphragms, cervical caps, vaults; spermicidal creams/jellies

Intrauterine devices: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375), hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20); action - phagocytosis of sperms, suppressed motility, uterus unsuitable for implantation
Oral contraceptives: progestogens or progestogen-oestrogen pills taken daily for 21 days; inhibit ovulation and implantation, alter cervical mucus; Saheli (non-steroidal, weekly; CDRI Lucknow)
Injections and implants of progestogens/oestrogens; emergency contraceptives within 72 hours of coitus
Surgical/terminal methods (sterilisation): vasectomy and tubectomy; highly effective but poorly reversible
Side effects of contraceptives: nausea, abdominal pain, irregular bleeding, possible breast cancer risk
MTP (induced abortion) before full term; about 45-50 million cases per year worldwide
MTP Amendment Act 2017 legal conditions: up to 12 weeks with one registered medical practitioner; 12-24 weeks with two practitioners' opinion on specific grounds
Uses: unwanted pregnancies, risk to mother or foetus; safest in first trimester
Concerns: misuse for female foeticide, unqualified quacks, emotional/ethical/social issues
STIs/VD/RTI examples: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B, HIV/AIDS
Hepatitis-B and HIV also spread by sharing needles, blood transfusion, infected mother to foetus; others curable when detected early
Early symptoms (itching, discharge, pain, swelling) and complications: PID, abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, cancer of reproductive tract
Prevention: avoid sex with unknown/multiple partners, use condoms, consult a doctor early; most common in 15-24 age group
Infertility: inability to conceive after two years of unprotected cohabitation; causes physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological, psychological
Assisted reproductive technologies (ART): IVF followed by embryo transfer (ET) - 'test tube baby' programme
ZIFT: zygote or early embryo (up to 8 blastomeres) into fallopian tube; IUT: embryo with more than 8 blastomeres into uterus
In vivo fertilisation within female, GIFT: transfer of ovum from donor into fallopian tube
ICSI: sperm directly injected into ovum
Artificial insemination (AI) and intra-uterine insemination (IUI) for low sperm count
Limitations: specialised professionals, costly, emotional/religious/social factors; adoption as an alternative
Exercise type: list features of an ideal contraceptive; classify contraceptive methods with examples; explain amniocentesis ban
Exercise type: expand and explain ART abbreviations (IVF, ZIFT, GIFT, ICSI, IUI, IUT); state measures for preventing STIs
Inheritance: transmission of characters from parent to progeny; variation: degree of difference between progeny and parents
Genetics as the branch dealing with inheritance and variation; early artificial selection and domestication (Sahiwal cows)
Gregor Mendel's hybridisation experiments on garden pea (1856-1863); statistical analysis and large samples
True-breeding lines; seven pairs of contrasting traits in pea (stem height, flower colour, pod shape/colour, seed shape/colour, flower position)
Monohybrid cross of tall and dwarf plants: F1 all tall, F2 3:1 phenotypic ratio
Factors (genes), alleles; homozygous vs heterozygous; genotype vs phenotype; dominant and recessive traits
Punnett square method (Reginald C. Punnett) to work out F2 genotypes; genotypic ratio 1:2:1
Test cross: cross with recessive parent to determine genotype of a dominant-phenotype organism
4.2.1 Law of dominance: characters controlled by discrete factors occurring in pairs; one dominates in a dissimilar pair
4.2.2 Law of segregation: alleles separate during gamete formation; gametes pure for a trait
4.2.2.1 Incomplete dominance: F1 intermediate phenotype (dog flower/snapdragon - red, pink, white; F2 1:2:1 both phenotypically and genotypically)
Concept of dominance explained by gene products: functional enzyme vs non-functional/less efficient allele
4.2.2.2 Co-dominance: both alleles expressed in heterozygote (ABO blood groups - IA, IB, i alleles)
Multiple allelism: more than two alleles of a gene in a population; six genotypes and four phenotypes of ABO groups
Starch grain size in pea seeds as example where dominance depends on trait examined
Numerical type: predict ratios and genotypes from monohybrid crosses and blood-group crosses
Dihybrid cross: round yellow x wrinkled green; F2 phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1
4.3.1 Law of independent assortment: segregation of one pair of characters is independent of another
Numerical type: dihybrid Punnett square (16 boxes), genotypic ratios and probability of specific genotypes
4.3.2 Chromosomal theory of inheritance: rediscovery of Mendel's work (de Vries, Correns, von Tschermak, 1900); Sutton and Boveri united chromosome movement with Mendel's laws
Parallel behaviour of genes and chromosomes during meiosis (pairs, segregation, independent assortment)
T.H. Morgan's experimental verification using Drosophila melanogaster - reasons for suitability (short life cycle, many progeny, visible variations)
4.3.3 Linkage and recombination: Morgan's dihybrid crosses on sex-linked genes (body colour, eye colour, wing size)
Linkage: physical association of genes on a chromosome; recombination: generation of non-parental gene combinations
Tightly linked genes show low recombination; Alfred Sturtevant used recombination frequency for gene mapping
Traits controlled by three or more genes with additive effects; continuous variation (human height, skin colour)
Environmental influence on polygenic traits; skin colour example with three genes (A, B, C)
One gene affecting multiple phenotypic expressions via effect on metabolic pathways
Example: phenylketonuria - single gene mutation causing mental retardation and reduced hair/skin pigmentation
Henking's X-body in insects; sex chromosomes vs autosomes
XO type (grasshopper: males XO), XY type (Drosophila, humans) - male heterogamety
ZW type (birds): female heterogamety (ZW female, ZZ male)
4.6.1 Sex determination in humans: XY mechanism; 50% probability of male/female child; sperm decides sex

Sex determination in honey bee: haplodiploid system - fertilised eggs become females (queen/workers), unfertilised eggs develop parthenogenetically into males (drones); males have no father and cannot have sons
Exercise type: explain why the father is responsible for the child's sex; pedigree of honey bee
Mutation: alteration in DNA sequence changing genotype and phenotype; source of variation
Chromosomal aberrations: deletions, insertions/duplications of DNA segments; cancer cell aberrations
Point mutation: single base pair change (sickle-cell anaemia); frameshift via insertion/deletion
Mutagens: chemical and physical factors (UV radiation)
4.8.1 Pedigree analysis: study of a trait across family generations; standard pedigree symbols
Interpreting pedigrees: autosomal dominant (myotonic dystrophy), autosomal recessive (sickle-cell anaemia)
4.8.2 Mendelian disorders: caused by single gene alteration; dominant/recessive, autosomal/sex-linked
Haemophilia: sex-linked recessive; defective clotting protein; carrier females, mostly affected males; Queen Victoria's family
Sickle-cell anaemia: autosomal recessive; Glu to Val substitution at 6th position of beta-globin (GAG to GUG); sickle-shaped RBCs under low O2; HbA HbS carriers
Phenylketonuria: autosomal recessive; lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase; phenylpyruvic acid accumulation

Thalassemia: autosomal recessive blood disorder; alpha thalassemia (HBA1, HBA2 on chromosome 16) and beta thalassemia (HBB on chromosome 11); quantitative problem (too few globins) vs sickle-cell qualitative problem
Colour blindness: sex-linked recessive (X chromosome); red/green cone defect; ~8% males, 0.4% females
4.8.3 Chromosomal disorders: aneuploidy (failure of chromatid segregation) vs polyploidy (failure of cytokinesis, common in plants)
Down's syndrome: trisomy 21; short stature, round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, palm crease, retarded development (Langdon Down, 1866)
Klinefelter's syndrome: 47, XXY; overall masculine with feminine features (gynaecomastia), sterile
Turner's syndrome: 45, X0; sterile females, rudimentary ovaries, lack of secondary sexual characters
Exercise type: solve pedigree charts to identify inheritance pattern and genotypes
Exercise type: cross problems on haemophilia/colour blindness (carrier mother x normal father)
Exercise type: distinguish dominance, co-dominance and incomplete dominance; linkage vs crossing over; aneuploidy vs polyploidy
DNA and RNA as two types of nucleic acids; DNA as genetic material in most organisms, RNA in some viruses; RNA as messenger/adapter/structural/catalytic
DNA as long polymer of deoxyribonucleotides; length expressed in base pairs (phi X174 5386 nt, lambda phage 48502 bp, E. coli 4.6 x 10^6 bp, human haploid 3.3 x 10^9 bp)
5.1.1 Structure of polynucleotide chain: nucleoside (base + pentose via N-glycosidic bond), nucleotide (+ phosphate via phosphoester bond), 3'-5' phosphodiester linkage; 5' and 3' ends
Friedrich Meischer identified 'nuclein'; Wilkins and Franklin X-ray diffraction data
Watson-Crick double helix (1953): two antiparallel chains, sugar-phosphate backbone, complementary base pairing (A=T two H-bonds, G-C three H-bonds), Chargaff's rule
Helix features: right-handed coiling, pitch 3.4 nm, ~10 bp per turn, 0.34 nm between bp; base stacking
Central dogma (Francis Crick): DNA -> RNA -> protein; reverse transcription in some viruses
Numerical type: calculate DNA length from bp number or base percentages using Chargaff's rule
5.1.2 Packaging of DNA helix: prokaryotic nucleoid with DNA held by positively charged proteins
Eukaryotic packaging: histones (lysine and arginine rich) form histone octamer; nucleosome (~200 bp) - 'beads on string'
Chromatin fibres coil into chromosomes at metaphase; non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins; euchromatin (loosely packed, active) vs heterochromatin (dense, inactive)
5.2.1 Transforming principle: Frederick Griffith (1928) - S and R strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae in mice; heat-killed S + live R transformed R strain
5.2.2 Biochemical characterisation of transforming principle: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed DNA (not protein/RNA) caused transformation; DNase stops transformation
5.2.3 The genetic material is DNA: Hershey and Chase (1952) experiment with bacteriophages grown on radioactive phosphorus (32P DNA) and sulphur (35S protein); blending and centrifugation
5.2.4 Properties of genetic material: replication, chemical and structural stability, scope for slow mutation, ability to express as Mendelian characters
Why DNA is more stable than RNA: 2'-OH in RNA makes it reactive; thymine in DNA adds stability; RNA mutates faster and can catalyse
DNA preferred for storage of genetic information; RNA better for transmission (needs protein synthesis)
RNA was the first genetic material; acted as genetic material and catalyst
Evolution of DNA from RNA via chemical modifications for stability; DNA double-stranded with complementary strand for repair
Semi-conservative replication proposed by Watson and Crick: each strand as template
5.4.1 The experimental proof: Meselson and Stahl (1958) with 15N/14N E. coli and CsCl density gradient centrifugation - hybrid then light/hybrid bands
Taylor's experiment on Vicia faba with radioactive thymidine showing semi-conservative replication in chromosomes
5.4.2 The machinery and the enzymes: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase; high speed and fidelity; energy from deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates
Replication fork; polymerisation only in 5'->3' direction: continuous leading strand vs discontinuous lagging strand (Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase)
Origin of replication (ori); replication coupled with cell cycle (S phase); failure of cell division causes polyploidy
Transcription: copying genetic information from one DNA strand into RNA; only a segment and only one strand transcribed
Reasons only one strand transcribed: two different proteins would result; dsRNA would prevent translation
5.5.1 Transcription unit: promoter (upstream, 5' end of coding strand), structural gene, terminator (downstream)
Template strand (3'->5') vs coding strand (5'->3', same sequence as RNA except T for U)
5.5.2 Transcription unit and the gene: cistron as DNA segment coding a polypeptide; monocistronic (eukaryotes) vs polycistronic (bacteria)
Split genes in eukaryotes: exons (expressed sequences) interrupted by introns (intervening sequences)
5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of transcription: mRNA (template), tRNA (adapter), rRNA (structural and catalytic)
Bacterial transcription by single RNA polymerase: initiation (sigma factor), elongation, termination (rho factor); coupled transcription and translation
Eukaryotic RNA polymerases: RNA Pol I (rRNAs 28S, 18S, 5.8S), RNA Pol II (hnRNA precursor of mRNA), RNA Pol III (tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs)
Post-transcriptional processing of hnRNA: splicing (introns removed), capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate at 5'), tailing (poly-A at 3')
Genetic code: relationship between nucleotide sequence on mRNA and amino acid sequence; George Gamow proposed triplet code
Har Gobind Khorana's chemical method for RNA with defined bases; Marshall Nirenberg's cell-free system; Severo Ochoa enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase)

Properties: triplet codon; 61 code for amino acids, 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); unambiguous and specific; degenerate; read contiguously (no punctuation); nearly universal; AUG dual function (methionine and initiator)
Codon table reading exercises
5.6.1 Mutations and genetic code: point mutation in beta-globin gene (sickle-cell); frameshift insertion/deletion mutations demonstrated with sentence analogy ('RAM HAS RED CAP')
5.6.2 tRNA - the adapter molecule: anticodon loop, amino acid acceptor end; clover-leaf secondary structure and inverted L 3-D shape; initiator tRNA; no tRNA for stop codons
Translation: polymerisation of amino acids into polypeptide; peptide bond formation needs energy
Charging (aminoacylation) of tRNA using ATP
Ribosome: large and small subunits; 23S rRNA acts as ribozyme (peptidyl transferase) in bacteria
Untranslated regions (UTRs) at 5' and 3' ends; start codon AUG and stop codons
Steps: initiation (small subunit binds mRNA, initiator tRNA), elongation (aminoacyl-tRNA entry, peptide bond, ribosome moves codon by codon), termination (release factor at stop codon)
Regulation levels in eukaryotes: transcriptional (primary transcript formation), processing (splicing), mRNA transport, translational
Regulation in prokaryotes mainly at transcription initiation; accessibility of promoter controlled by accessory proteins (activators, repressors) via operators
5.8.1 The lac operon (Francois Jacob and Jacques Monod): polycistronic structural genes regulated by a common promoter and regulatory gene
lac operon components: regulatory gene i (repressor), structural genes z (beta-galactosidase), y (permease), a (transacetylase)
Lactose as inducer: binds repressor and inactivates it, allowing transcription; absence of inducer - repressor binds operator, operon switched off
Negative regulation of lac operon by repressor; also positive regulation (mentioned)
HGP launched 1990, completed 2003; mega project; estimated cost $3 per bp; storage requirements discussed
Goals: identify all ~20,000-25,000 genes, sequence 3 billion bp, store information, improve analysis tools, transfer technology, address ELSI (ethical, legal, social issues)
Coordinated by US Department of Energy and NIH; Wellcome Trust (UK) and contributions from Japan, France, Germany, China
Applications: understanding human biology, disease diagnosis and treatment; non-human model organisms sequenced (bacteria, yeast, C. elegans, Drosophila, rice, Arabidopsis)
5.9.1 Methodologies: Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs) vs sequence annotation
Sequencing method: random fragmentation, cloning in host using vectors (BAC, YAC), Frederick Sanger's automated sequencing, overlapping fragment alignment by computer programs
Genetic and physical maps using restriction endonuclease recognition sites and microsatellites
5.9.2 Salient features of human genome: 3164.7 million bp; average gene 3000 bases (dystrophin largest, 2.4 million bases); ~30,000 genes; 99.9% identical between individuals
Unknown function for over 50% of discovered genes; less than 2% codes for proteins; repetitive sequences; chromosome 1 most genes (2968), Y fewest (231); ~1.4 million SNPs identified
5.9.3 Applications and future challenges: studying all genes and transcripts at once; understanding complex biological processes
DNA fingerprinting compares repetitive DNA sequences between individuals; developed by Alec Jeffreys
Repetitive DNA separates as satellite DNA in density gradient centrifugation; classified as micro-/mini-satellites; VNTRs as probes
Polymorphism (variation at genetic level) arising from mutations, inherited between generations
Steps: isolation of DNA, digestion by restriction endonucleases, separation by electrophoresis, Southern blotting to membranes, hybridisation with labelled VNTR probe, detection by autoradiography
VNTR size varies (0.1-20 kb); inheritance of VNTR bands from parents
Applications: forensic science, paternity testing, population and genetic diversity studies; PCR increases sensitivity
Exercise type: draw schematic of a polynucleotide/nucleosome/replication fork/transcription unit/lac operon
Exercise type: write mRNA from a given DNA template, or amino acid sequence from mRNA using codon table; identify effect of mutations
Exercise type: explain Hershey-Chase and Meselson-Stahl experiments; list goals of HGP; describe DNA fingerprinting steps
Big Bang theory of universe origin; Earth formed ~4.5 billion years ago; early atmosphere (water vapour, methane, CO2, ammonia)
Life appeared ~500 million years after Earth's formation (about 4 billion years ago)
Panspermia: spores from outer space; spontaneous generation theory dismissed by Louis Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments
Oparin and Haldane: first life from pre-existing non-living organic molecules via chemical evolution
S.L. Miller's experiment (1953): electric discharge in CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 C formed amino acids; similar experiments formed sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats
First non-cellular forms of life ~3 billion years ago; first cellular forms ~2000 million years ago

sections.name: 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms - A Theory

concepts.text: Special creation theory's three connotations (all species created as is, unchanged since creation, Earth about 4000 years old) and its challenge in the 19th century
Charles Darwin's voyage on H.M.S. Beagle; observations of variation and extinct forms; Alfred Wallace's similar conclusions in Malay Archipelago
Fitness as reproductive fitness; natural selection explains evolution of life forms; common ancestry

sections.name: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

concepts.text: Palaeontological evidence: fossils in sedimentary rock layers; radioactive dating of fossils
Comparative anatomy - homologous organs (divergent evolution): forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and human; heart and brain of vertebrates; thorn and tendrils in Bougainvillea and Cucurbita
Analogous organs (convergent evolution): wings of butterfly and bird; eyes of octopus and mammals; flippers of penguins and dolphins; sweet potato (root) and potato (stem)
Molecular homology: similarities in proteins and genes indicate common ancestry
Embryological evidence (Ernst Haeckel) of gill slits in vertebrate embryos and its disproval by Karl Ernst von Baer
Natural selection in action: industrial melanism in peppered moths (Biston betularia) in England
Anthropogenic selection: herbicide/pesticide resistance, antibiotic resistance in microbes; artificial selection in domestication (dog breeds)
Adaptive radiation: evolution of different species in a geographical area from one point, radiating into other habitats
Darwin's finches of Galapagos Islands: seed-eating ancestor evolved varied beaks (insectivorous, vegetarian)
Australian marsupials radiating from a common ancestor; convergent evolution between placental mammals and marsupials (wolf/Tasmanian wolf etc.)
Natural selection based on heritable variation leading to differential reproduction; fitness and adaptation
Branching descent and natural selection as two key concepts of Darwinism
Exponential growth of populations; resource limits; competition and survival of better-adapted individuals
Hugo de Vries' mutation theory using evening primrose (Oenothera lamarckiana): saltation - single-step large mutations
Darwinian variations small and directional vs de Vries' random directionless mutations
Population genetics: mutation and recombination as source of variation; speciation
Allele frequencies in a population are stable and constant across generations without disturbance (genetic equilibrium)
Equation: p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1 (binomial expansion of (p+q)^2); gene pool concept
Factors disturbing equilibrium: gene migration/gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, natural selection
Founder effect: original drifted population becomes founders
Types of natural selection: stabilising (more individuals with mean value), directional (toward one extreme), disruptive (both extremes)
Numerical type: calculate allele and genotype frequencies using Hardy-Weinberg
Geological timescale overview: first cellular forms ~2000 mya; multicellular invertebrates ~500 mya
Jawless fish ~350 mya; lobefins (coelacanth) evolved into first amphibians; amphibians to reptiles (thick-shelled eggs)
Seed ferns, gymnosperms; dinosaurs and their extinction ~65 mya; Tyrannosaurus rex
Rise of mammals ~200 mya: shrews; pouched mammals of Australia; evolution of horse, elephant, dog etc.
Plant evolution sequence: Zosterophyllum, Psilophyton, ferns, gymnosperms, monocots and dicots (chart)
Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus (~15 mya) - hairy, gorilla/chimpanzee-like walk; Ramapithecus more man-like
Australopithecines (~2 mya) in East African grasslands: hunted with stone weapons, ate fruit
Homo habilis: first human-like being, brain 650-800 cc, probably did not eat meat
Homo erectus (~1.5 mya, Java man): brain ~900 cc, probably ate meat
Neanderthal man (100,000-40,000 years ago): brain 1400 cc, buried dead, lived in Near East and Central Asia
Homo sapiens arose in Africa and migrated; ice age 75,000-10,000 years ago; prehistoric cave art (18,000 years ago); agriculture ~10,000 years ago and settlements
Exercise type: differentiate homologous and analogous organs with examples; explain adaptive radiation; give Miller's experiment set-up
Exercise type: compare Darwin's and de Vries' views; Hardy-Weinberg numericals; arrange human ancestors by brain capacity and time
Health: state of complete physical, mental and social well-being; factors affecting health - genetic disorders, infections, lifestyle
Hippocrates' and Indian Ayurveda's 'good humour' views; William Harvey's discovery of blood circulation disproved humour theory
Infectious vs non-infectious diseases; AIDS and cancer as major killers; drug and alcohol abuse
Pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, helminths; adaptations to survive in host
Typhoid: Salmonella typhi; contaminated food/water; sustained fever, weakness, intestinal perforation; Widal test; Mary Mallon ('Typhoid Mary')
Pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; alveoli fill with fluid; fever, chills, cough, bluish lips/nails; droplets or shared utensils
Common cold: rhinoviruses; infects nose and respiratory passage (not lungs); droplet and contaminated object transmission
Malaria: Plasmodium vivax, P. malariae, P. falciparum (malignant, may be fatal)

Plasmodium life cycle: sporozoites from female Anopheles bite, multiply in liver then RBCs; haemozoin toxin causes chill and high fever every 3-4 days; gametocytes taken by mosquito; fertilisation in mosquito gut; sporozoites in salivary glands
Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery): Entamoeba histolytica in large intestine; constipation, cramps, mucoid stools; houseflies as mechanical carriers
Ascariasis: Ascaris (roundworm); internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, intestinal blockage; eggs via contaminated water/vegetables
Elephantiasis (filariasis): Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi; chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs and genital organs; Culex mosquito
Ringworm: Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton fungi; dry scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp; heat and moisture favour growth

Prevention and control: personal hygiene, public hygiene (waste disposal, water), avoiding contact, vector control (eliminating breeding sites, Gambusia fish, insecticides, nets), Aedes mosquitoes in dengue and chikungunya
Advances: vaccines and immunisation (smallpox eradicated), antibiotics, drugs
Immunity: ability of host to fight disease-causing organisms

7.2.1 Innate immunity: non-specific, present at birth; physical barriers (skin, mucus coating), physiological (stomach acid, saliva, tears), cellular (PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes, NK cells, macrophages), cytokine barriers (interferons)
7.2.2 Acquired immunity: pathogen-specific and memory-based; primary vs anamnestic secondary response
B-lymphocytes produce antibodies; T-lymphocytes help B cells; antibody structure H2L2 (two heavy, two light chains); types IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG
Humoral (antibody-mediated) vs cell-mediated immune response (T cells); graft/organ rejection; tissue and blood group matching; immunosuppressants
7.2.3 Active and passive immunity: active - host's own antibodies (slow); passive - ready-made antibodies (colostrum IgA, placenta IgG to foetus, anti-tetanus serum, snake antivenom)
7.2.4 Vaccination and immunisation: inactivated/weakened pathogens or antigenic proteins generate memory B and T cells; recombinant DNA vaccines (hepatitis B from yeast)
7.2.5 Allergies: exaggerated response to allergens (mites in dust, pollen, animal dander); IgE antibodies; histamine and serotonin from mast cells; antihistamines, adrenaline, steroids
7.2.6 Auto immunity: immune system attacks self cells (rheumatoid arthritis)

7.2.7 Immune system in the body: primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow, thymus) and secondary lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix); MALT forms ~50% of lymphoid tissue
Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome; first reported in 1981; caused by HIV (retrovirus with RNA genome)
Transmission: sexual contact with infected person, transfusion of contaminated blood, sharing needles, infected mother to child via placenta
HIV life cycle: enters macrophage, RNA copied to viral DNA by reverse transcriptase, incorporated into host DNA; macrophages as HIV factory; attacks helper T-lymphocytes (TH cells)
Incubation period from a few months to 5-10 years; decreasing TH count leads to opportunistic infections (Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi, Toxoplasma)
Diagnosis by ELISA; anti-retroviral drugs partially effective
Prevention: NACO, educating people, safe blood, disposable needles, free condoms, controlling drug abuse; 'don't die of ignorance'
Cancer: loss of contact inhibition causes uncontrolled cell proliferation forming tumours
Benign tumours (confined, little damage) vs malignant tumours (neoplastic cells invade tissues); metastasis spreads via blood
Causes of cancer (carcinogens): physical (X-rays, gamma rays, UV), chemical (tobacco smoke), biological (oncogenic viruses with viral oncogenes); proto-oncogenes/cellular oncogenes

Cancer detection and diagnosis: biopsy and histopathology, blood and bone marrow tests for leukaemia, radiography (X-rays), CT, MRI, antibodies against cancer-specific antigens, molecular biology for genetic susceptibility
Treatment: surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy (side effects like hair loss, anaemia), immunotherapy with biological response modifiers (alpha-interferon)
Opioids: bind opioid receptors in CNS and GI tract; heroin (smack, diacetylmorphine) from morphine extracted from poppy latex (Papaver somniferum); depressant
Cannabinoids: from Cannabis sativa inflorescences (marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja); affect cardiovascular system; used to enhance sports performance (abuse)
Coca alkaloid/cocaine from Erythroxylum coca: interferes with dopamine transport; euphoria, hallucinations; Atropa belladonna and Datura as hallucinogenic plants
Drugs with medicinal use misused: barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, LSD; morphine as sedative/painkiller

Tobacco: nicotine stimulates adrenal gland (adrenaline, noradrenaline) raising blood pressure and heart rate; smoking linked to cancers, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease; increased carbon monoxide in blood
7.5.1 Adolescence and drug/alcohol abuse: adolescence as period of 12-18 years; reasons for use - curiosity, adventure, excitement, peer pressure, stress, family problems
7.5.2 Addiction and dependence: psychological attachment to euphoria; tolerance; withdrawal syndrome when intake stops

7.5.3 Effects of drug/alcohol abuse: reckless behaviour, vandalism, violence, coma, death from overdose; liver cirrhosis, nervous system damage; foetal effects; HIV/hepatitis B by needles; anabolic steroid side effects in males and females
Warning signs of drug abuse: drop in academic performance, absence, poor hygiene, withdrawal, isolation, depression, change in sleeping/eating habits
7.5.4 Prevention and control: avoid undue peer pressure, education and counselling, seek help from parents and peers, look for danger signs, professional and medical help
Exercise type: match disease with pathogen and symptoms; explain Plasmodium life cycle; compare active and passive immunity
Exercise type: explain how HIV causes immune deficiency; differentiate benign and malignant tumours; list adverse effects of drugs; define B/T cells and antibodies
Microbes are ubiquitous - soil, water, air, hot springs (thermal vents up to 100 C), deep soil, under snow, acidic environments, inside organisms
Diversity of microbes: protozoa, bacteria, fungi, microscopic algae, viruses, viroids, prions; growth on nutrient media as colonies
Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria, LAB) converts milk to curd; improves vitamin B12; checks disease-causing microbes in stomach
Fermentation of dough for dosa and idli by bacteria; bread dough leavened by baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae)
Toddy from fermented palm sap; fermented fish, soyabean and bamboo shoot products
Cheese-making: Propionibacterium sharmanii gives large holes in Swiss cheese; Roquefort cheese ripened by specific fungi
8.2.1 Fermented beverages: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast) for wine, beer, whisky, brandy, rum; distilled vs non-distilled drinks
8.2.2 Antibiotics: chemicals produced by microbes that kill/retard growth of other microbes; penicillin discovered by Alexander Fleming from Penicillium notatum; full potential by Chain and Florey
Antibiotics used to treat plague, whooping cough, diphtheria, leprosy

8.2.3 Chemicals, enzymes and other bioactive molecules: citric acid (Aspergillus niger), acetic acid (Acetobacter aceti), butyric acid (Clostridium butylicum), lactic acid (Lactobacillus); ethanol from yeast
Enzymes: lipases in detergents, pectinases and proteases to clarify bottled juices, streptokinase from Streptococcus as clot buster
Cyclosporin A from Trichoderma polysporum as immunosuppressant in organ transplants; statins from Monascus purpureus as blood-cholesterol lowering agents (competitive inhibition)
Sewage: municipal waste-water with organic matter and microbes; treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) before release
Primary treatment: physical removal of particles by filtration and sedimentation; primary sludge and effluent
Secondary (biological) treatment: aeration tanks, growth of aerobic microbes into flocs (bacteria + fungal filaments); BOD reduction
BOD (biochemical oxygen demand): amount of O2 consumed if all organic matter in 1 L water oxidised by bacteria; measure of organic pollution
Settling tank: activated sludge; part returned to aeration tank as inoculum; remainder to anaerobic sludge digesters producing biogas (methane, H2S, CO2)
Effluent from secondary treatment released into rivers; Ganga Action Plan and Yamuna Action Plan by Ministry of Environment and Forests
Biogas: mixture of gases (mainly methane) produced by microbial activity; used as fuel
Methanogens (e.g. Methanobacterium) grow anaerobically on cellulosic material; found in sludge and rumen of cattle; cattle dung (gobar) rich in them
Biogas plant: concrete tank (10-15 ft deep), slurry of dung, floating cover rising with gas, outlet pipe; spent slurry as fertiliser
Technology developed by IARI and KVIC; rural energy use
Biocontrol: using biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests; reduces chemical pesticide use; organic farming and holistic approach
Predators as natural controls: ladybird and dragonflies for aphids and mosquitoes
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spores sprayed to kill butterfly caterpillars; Bt toxin genes introduced into plants
Trichoderma fungi as biocontrol agents of plant pathogens in root ecosystems
Baculoviruses (genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus) as species-specific narrow-spectrum insecticides; useful in IPM
Biofertilisers: organisms that enrich soil nutrient quality; reduce chemical fertiliser pollution
Rhizobium in root nodules of leguminous plants fixes atmospheric nitrogen symbiotically
Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria: Azospirillum and Azotobacter
Mycorrhiza: fungal symbiosis (genus Glomus) absorbs phosphorus, provides resistance to root pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought
Cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria) as autotrophic N-fixers in paddy fields; add organic matter to soil
Exercise type: name microbes for given products (citric acid, cyclosporin A, statins, streptokinase, Swiss cheese)
Exercise type: explain primary and secondary sewage treatment; define BOD and interpret BOD data; describe biogas plant
Exercise type: list benefits of biofertilisers and biocontrol over chemical methods
Biotechnology: using live organisms or enzymes to make useful products; EFB definition integrating natural science and organisms/cells for products and services
Traditional (curd, bread, wine) vs modern biotechnology (genetically modified organisms)
Core techniques: genetic engineering (altering genetic material) and bioprocess engineering (sterile, contamination-free growth of microbes/cells)
Limitations of traditional hybridisation; asexual vs sexual reproduction in preserving/varying genetic information
Steps of genetically modifying an organism: identify DNA with desirable genes, introduce into host, maintain introduced DNA and transfer to progeny
Origin of replication (ori) needed for DNA replication in host; plasmids as autonomously replicating DNA
First recombinant DNA by Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer (1972): antibiotic resistance gene linked to Salmonella typhimurium plasmid
Molecular scissors (restriction enzymes) and DNA ligase; cloning - multiple identical copies of template DNA
9.2.1 Restriction enzymes: first restriction endonuclease Hind II (1963) cuts at specific six-bp sequence (recognition sequence)
Naming convention: EcoRI - genus (E), species (co), strain (R), order of isolation (I)
Nucleases: exonucleases (remove nucleotides from ends) vs endonucleases (cut within DNA)
Palindromic recognition sequences read same on both strands in same orientation (e.g. 5'-GAATTC-3')
Sticky ends: overhanging single-stranded ends from cuts slightly away from centre; join with complementary ends via DNA ligase
Separation and isolation of DNA fragments: agarose gel electrophoresis; negatively charged DNA moves to anode; sieving effect separates by size
Visualising DNA with ethidium bromide under UV (orange bands); elution of bands for cloning
9.2.2 Cloning vectors: plasmids and bacteriophages; high copy number
Features of cloning vectors: origin of replication (controls copy number); selectable marker (ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, kanamycin resistance genes)
Cloning (recognition) sites: unique sites within vector; insertional inactivation (tetR, ampR in pBR322)
Insertional inactivation of beta-galactosidase gene: blue vs colourless colonies with chromogenic substrate
Vectors for cloning genes in plants and animals: Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens modified as non-pathogenic vector; disarmed retroviruses in animals
9.2.3 Competent host (for transformation with rDNA): making cells competent by divalent cations (calcium); heat shock (ice, 42 C, ice) to take up rDNA
Other methods: micro-injection into animal nucleus; biolistics/gene gun (gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA) for plants; disarmed pathogen vectors
Overview steps: isolation of DNA, fragmentation by restriction enzymes, isolation of desired fragment, ligation into vector, transfer into host, culturing host, product extraction
9.3.1 Isolation of the genetic material (DNA): cell lysis with lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plants), chitinase (fungi); removal of RNA (ribonuclease), proteins (protease), and lipids
Precipitation of purified DNA by chilled ethanol; spooling of fine threads
9.3.2 Cutting of DNA at specific locations: restriction digestion checked by agarose gel electrophoresis; vector cut with same enzyme
9.3.3 Amplification of gene of interest using PCR: polymerase chain reaction steps - denaturation, annealing of primers, extension
Thermostable Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus; ~1 billion copies after 30 cycles; amplified fragment ligated with vector
9.3.4 Insertion of recombinant DNA into host cell/organism: selection of transformants by antibiotic resistance markers
9.3.5 Obtaining the foreign gene product: recombinant protein; heterologous host expression; small-scale vs large-scale culture
Bioreactors: vessels (100-1000 L) for large-scale culture; optimal conditions - temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen
Stirred-tank bioreactor: curved base, agitator, oxygen delivery (sparger), foam control, temperature/pH control, sampling ports; simple vs sparged stirred-tank designs
9.3.6 Downstream processing: separation and purification of product; formulation with preservatives; clinical trials and quality control
Exercise type: identify palindromic sequences and restriction sites; write sticky ends after EcoRI cut
Exercise type: label pBR322 and explain selectable markers/insertional inactivation; describe PCR steps and gel electrophoresis
Exercise type: explain methods of introducing rDNA into host; list features of an ideal vector and bioreactor
Applications of biotechnology: therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, energy production
Critical research areas: best catalyst (organism/enzyme), optimal conditions for catalyst, downstream processing
Three options for increasing food production: agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture, genetically engineered crop-based agriculture
Green Revolution's limits; use of GMOs (genetically modified organisms) as alternative

Benefits of GM plants: tolerance to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), reduced reliance on pesticides, reduced post-harvest losses, efficient mineral use, enhanced nutritional value (Golden rice - vitamin A)
Pest-resistant plants reduce pesticide use; tailor-made plants supply alternative resources (starch, fuels, pharmaceuticals)
Bt toxin from Bacillus thuringiensis; Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato, soyabean
Mechanism: inactive protoxin crystals become active in alkaline insect gut, bind midgut epithelium, create pores causing cell swelling and lysis
cry genes coding Bt toxin: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; cryIAb controls corn borer
Pest-resistant plants using RNA interference (RNAi): silencing specific mRNA by complementary dsRNA
Meloidogyne incognita (nematode) infecting tobacco roots; Agrobacterium vectors introduce nematode-specific genes producing sense and anti-sense RNA, forming dsRNA that silences parasite mRNA
rDNA technology enables safe, effective therapeutic drugs; about 30 recombinant therapeutics approved worldwide, 12 in India
10.2.1 Genetically engineered insulin: insulin from slaughtered cattle/pigs caused allergies; insulin structure - A and B chains linked by disulphide bridges; pro-insulin with extra C peptide
Eli Lilly (1983) prepared DNA sequences for A and B chains, introduced into E. coli plasmids; chains combined by disulphide bonds to form human insulin
10.2.2 Gene therapy: correcting a gene defect diagnosed in a child/embryo by introducing normal genes
First clinical gene therapy (1990) for adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency - immune system disorder; enzyme replacement therapy and bone-marrow transplantation alternatives

Gene therapy steps: lymphocytes cultured, functional ADA cDNA introduced via retroviral vector, returned to patient; periodic infusion needed; permanent cure if gene introduced into early embryonic cells
10.2.3 Molecular diagnosis: early detection with PCR (HIV in suspected AIDS patients, cancer mutations, genetic disorders)
Single-stranded DNA/RNA probes tagged with radioactive molecules hybridise to complementary DNA; detected by autoradiography; mutated genes don't hybridise
ELISA based on antigen-antibody interaction to detect pathogens' antigens or antibodies
Transgenic animals: animals whose DNA is manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene; rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows, fish; over 95% are mice
Uses - normal physiology and development: study of gene regulation and effects (e.g. insulin-like growth factor)
Study of disease: models for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's
Biological products: alpha-1-antitrypsin for emphysema; Rosie the transgenic cow (1997) produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 g/L, alpha-lactalbumin)
Vaccine safety testing (polio vaccine on transgenic mice) and chemical safety (toxicity) testing

Genetic modification may have unpredictable results in ecosystems; Indian Government's GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) decides validity of GM research and safety of GM organisms for public use
Patents on biological resources; biopiracy - use of bio-resources by multinational companies without authorisation or compensation to the country/people
Basmati rice patent by an American company (1997); attempts to patent turmeric and neem uses
Traditional knowledge of developing countries; need for laws to prevent unauthorised exploitation; Indian Parliament's second amendment of Indian Patents Bill
Exercise type: explain how Bt toxin kills insects but not bacteria; describe RNAi mechanism and its use in pest control
Exercise type: outline production of human insulin and gene therapy for ADA deficiency; list uses of transgenic animals; define biopiracy with examples
Ecology: study of interactions among organisms and between organisms and their physical (abiotic) environment
Four levels of biological organisation in ecology: organisms, populations, communities, biomes (note: 'Organism and its Environment', abiotic factors, responses and adaptations sections deleted)
Population: group of individuals of a species in a well-defined geographical area sharing or competing for resources and interbreeding
Population ecology links ecology to population genetics and evolution; natural selection acts at population level
Attributes of populations not shown by individuals: birth rate (natality), death rate (mortality), sex ratio
Numerical type: calculate per capita birth rate and death rate (e.g. 20 lotus plants last year, 8 new; 4 of 40 fruit flies die per week)
Age pyramids: pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive groups; expanding (triangular), stable (bell-shaped), declining (urn-shaped) human population pyramids
Population size/density (N) measures: number, percent cover/biomass, relative density (fish caught per trap), indirect estimation (pug marks, faecal pellets of tigers)
Four basic processes changing population density: natality (B), mortality (D), immigration (I), emigration (E)
Equation: Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) - (D + E)]
Growth models - (i) exponential growth: unlimited resources; dN/dt = rN; Nt = N0 e^(rt); J-shaped curve
Intrinsic rate of natural increase (r): e.g. Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12; Indian population r in 1981 = 0.0205
(ii) Logistic growth: limited resources, carrying capacity (K); Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth dN/dt = rN[(K-N)/K]
Sigmoid curve phases: lag, acceleration, deceleration, asymptote at K; logistic model is more realistic
Graph interpretation: compare J-shaped and S-shaped curves
Populations evolve to maximise reproductive fitness (Darwinian fitness, high r) under given selection pressures
Breeding patterns: breed once in a lifetime (Pacific salmon, bamboo) vs many times (most birds and mammals); many small offspring (oysters, pelagic fishes) vs few large ones (birds, mammals)
Interspecific interactions table: mutualism (+,+), competition (-,-), predation (+,-), parasitism (+,-), commensalism (+,0), amensalism (-,0)

Predation: transfers energy across trophic levels; keeps prey populations under control (prickly pear cactus in Australia controlled by moth); maintains species diversity (Pisaster starfish removal experiment)

Prey defences: camouflage (cryptic colouring in frogs, insects), poisonous monarch butterfly (toxin from weed), thorns (Acacia, cactus), chemicals (Calotropis cardiac glycosides); plant secondary metabolites (nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium)
Competition: between related or unrelated species for limited resources (flamingos and fishes for zooplankton); interference competition
Competitive release (Connell's barnacle experiment - Balanus vs Chathamalus on Scottish coast); Abingdon tortoise extinction after goats introduced on Galapagos
Gause's competitive exclusion principle: two closely related species competing for same resources cannot coexist indefinitely
Resource partitioning: MacArthur's five warbler species foraging differently on same tree
Parasitism: host-specific parasites co-evolve; adaptations - loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs/suckers, loss of digestive system, high reproductive capacity
Complex life cycles of parasites (human liver fluke with snail and fish intermediate hosts; malaria parasite with mosquito vector); harmful effects on host
Ectoparasites (lice, ticks, copepods, Cuscuta) vs endoparasites; brood parasitism (cuckoo laying eggs in crow's nest; egg mimicry)
Commensalism: orchid on mango branch, barnacles on whales, cattle egret with grazing cattle, sea anemone and clown fish
Mutualism: lichens (fungus + alga/cyanobacteria), mycorrhizae (fungi + roots), plant-animal pollination and seed dispersal; fig and wasp species-specific relationship
Sexual deceit in pollination: Mediterranean orchid Ophrys mimics female bee (pseudocopulation)
Exercise type: identify the type of interaction from given examples; give plant defences against herbivores; explain competitive exclusion
Exercise type: draw and explain age pyramids; derive or apply exponential and logistic growth equations; calculate birth/death rates
Ecosystem as a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact with each other and the physical environment
Range of ecosystem sizes; terrestrial (forest, grassland, desert) and aquatic (pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary) ecosystems; man-made ecosystems (crop fields, aquarium)
Structure: interaction of biotic and abiotic components; species composition and stratification (vertical distribution in forests - trees, shrubs, herbs)
Functions: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling

Pond as a self-sustainable example: abiotic components (water, dissolved substances, soil deposit), autotrophs (phytoplankton, algae, floating/submerged/marginal plants), consumers (zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms), decomposers (fungi, bacteria, flagellates)
Unidirectional energy movement towards higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as heat
Primary production: amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over time by plants in photosynthesis; g m^-2 or kcal m^-2 per unit time
Productivity as rate of biomass production (g m^-2 yr^-1 or kcal m^-2 yr^-1)
Gross primary productivity (GPP) vs net primary productivity: NPP = GPP - R (respiration losses)
NPP is available biomass for heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers); secondary productivity: rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers

Primary productivity depends on plant species, environmental factors, nutrients, photosynthetic capacity; annual NPP of biosphere ~170 billion tons (dry weight); oceans only ~55 billion tons despite 70% of surface
Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances (CO2, water, nutrients); earthworm as farmer's friend
Detritus: dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead animal remains including faecal matter
Steps: fragmentation (detritivores like earthworm), leaching (water-soluble nutrients into soil as salts), catabolism (bacterial and fungal enzymes)
Humification: formation of dark amorphous humus, resistant to microbial action, very slow decomposition, colloidal reservoir of nutrients
Mineralisation: humus degraded by microbes releasing inorganic nutrients

Factors regulating decomposition: chemical composition of detritus (slow with lignin and chitin; fast with nitrogen and water-soluble sugars) and climate (temperature and soil moisture; warm and moist favour, low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit)
Sun as the only source of energy except deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems; less than 50% of incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active (PAR)
Plants capture only 2-10% of PAR, sustaining the entire living world
Unidirectional energy flow from sun to producers to consumers; second law of thermodynamics - ecosystems need constant energy supply
Producers (green plants) vs consumers (herbivores - primary consumers; carnivores - secondary and tertiary consumers)
Grazing food chain (GFC): grass -> goat -> man; detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter, decomposers (saprotrophs) such as fungi and bacteria
In aquatic ecosystems GFC is the major conduit; in terrestrial ecosystems more energy flows through DFC
Food web: interconnection of food chains; trophic levels based on source of nutrition
Standing crop: mass of living material at each trophic level at a particular time (biomass, fresh or dry weight)
10 per cent law: only about 10% of energy transferred from one trophic level to the next; limits the number of trophic levels
Numerical type: calculate energy available at higher trophic levels using 10% law
Ecological pyramid: base represents producers (first trophic level), apex represents top consumers
Pyramid of number: generally upright (grassland); inverted in a tree ecosystem with insects
Pyramid of biomass: upright in terrestrial ecosystems; inverted in sea where phytoplankton biomass is less than fish
Pyramid of energy: always upright because energy decreases at each level and some is lost as heat
Limitations of ecological pyramids: ignore species belonging to two or more trophic levels, assume simple food chain, do not accommodate food webs, saprophytes not given a place
Exercise type: draw pyramids of number, biomass, energy for given ecosystems; explain why pyramid of energy is never inverted
Exercise type: distinguish GPP and NPP, grazing and detritus food chains, humification and mineralisation; describe pond ecosystem components
Note: ecological succession, nutrient cycling (carbon, phosphorus) and ecosystem services sections deleted
Biodiversity: term popularised by Edward Wilson; diversity at all levels of biological organisation
Genetic diversity: variation within a species over its range (Rauwolfia vomitoria reserpine variation; 50,000 strains of rice and 1000 varieties of mango in India)
Species diversity: diversity at species level (Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than Eastern Ghats)
Ecological diversity: diversity at ecosystem level (India's deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, alpine meadows vs Norway)
13.1.1 How many species are there on Earth and how many in India: IUCN (2004) - over 1.5 million described; Robert May's global estimate ~7 million
Proportions of species: insects over 70% of animals; fungi more species than all vertebrates combined; prokaryotes not fully counted due to culturing limitations
India: 2.4% of world land area but 8.1% of global species diversity; one of 12 megadiversity countries; ~45,000 plant and twice as many animal species recorded

13.1.2 Patterns of biodiversity - (i) Latitudinal gradients: diversity decreases from equator towards poles; tropics (23.5 N to 23.5 S) richest (Colombia ~1400 bird species vs New York 105, Greenland 56; Amazon rain forest)
Hypotheses for tropical diversity: speciation over long undisturbed evolutionary time, less seasonal and more constant environment, more solar energy and higher productivity
(ii) Species-area relationships: Alexander von Humboldt's observation; log S = log C + Z log A; rectangular hyperbola and straight line on log scale
Z (slope of regression) values 0.1-0.2 for most regions; steeper (0.6-1.2) for very large areas such as whole continents (frugivorous birds and mammals)
13.1.3 The importance of species diversity to the ecosystem: stability and productivity relationships; David Tilman's outdoor plots - more species, less year-to-year variation and higher productivity
Rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich): each species as a rivet in an airplane; loss of key species (key rivets) threatens ecosystem
13.1.4 Loss of biodiversity: IUCN Red List (2004) - 784 extinctions in last 500 years (dodo, quagga, thylacine, Steller's sea cow, three subspecies of tiger - Bali, Javan, Caspian)
Sixth extinction in progress: current rates 100-1000 times faster than pre-human times; 12% birds, 23% mammals, 32% amphibians, 31% gymnosperms facing extinction
Effects of biodiversity loss: decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations, increased variability in ecosystem processes (productivity, water use, disease cycles)
Causes of biodiversity loss ('The Evil Quartet'): habitat loss and fragmentation (tropical rain forests reduced from 14% to 6% of land; Amazon converted for soybean and beef cattle)
Over-exploitation (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon; marine fish populations)

Alien species invasions: Nile perch in Lake Victoria (cichlid extinction); Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana, water hyacinth (Eichhornia); African catfish Clarias gariepinus threatening indigenous catfish
Co-extinctions: obligatory associations (host fish and parasites; plant-pollinator mutualism)

13.2.1 Why should we conserve biodiversity: narrowly utilitarian reasons - food, firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes), medicines (over 25% drugs from plants; 25,000 plant species used in traditional medicine)
Bioprospecting: exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for economically important products
Broadly utilitarian reasons: ecosystem services - Amazon producing ~20% of oxygen by photosynthesis, pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats; aesthetic pleasures
Ethical reasons: intrinsic value of every species; moral duty to pass on biological legacy
13.2.2 How do we conserve biodiversity: in situ (on site) conservation protects the whole ecosystem

Biodiversity hotspots: regions with high species richness and endemism; 34 hotspots worldwide; India's Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya; hotspots cover less than 2% of land but harbour vast species and could reduce extinctions by up to 30%
India's protected areas: 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 wildlife sanctuaries (figures as in book)

Sacred groves: tracts of forest set aside and protected by communities for religious reasons (Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, Sarguja/Chanda/Bastar of Madhya Pradesh)
Ex situ (off site) conservation: threatened animals and plants protected in zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks
Cryopreservation of gametes of threatened species; in vitro fertilisation; tissue culture propagation of plants; seed banks for commercially important plants

International efforts: Earth Summit (Rio de Janeiro, 1992) - Convention on Biological Diversity; World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, 2002) - commitment to reduce rate of biodiversity loss by 2010
Ramsar sites and Red Data Book (IUCN) as conservation tools (syllabus terms)
